messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Priya Chandrasekaran is a 73-year-old widowed South Asian woman who has spent the better part of four decades building a respected interior design practice in the Atlanta metropolitan area. Her work has always been tactile and sensory — she has made her living by running her hands across fabric swatches, feeling the grain of upholstery, selecting textures that communicate warmth or authority or calm. It is a bitter irony, then, that touch has become one of the things she most fears.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Priya was present at a peaceful community demonstration in her neighborhood, attending in solidarity with younger members of her local temple. What began as an orderly afternoon gathering escalated when a line of officers in full riot gear moved into the crowd. In the confusion, Priya was pushed to the ground, and as she attempted to rise, an officer pressed a knee and a gloved hand against her back and held her there on the pavement for what she estimates was several minutes. She recalls the coarse weave of her own jacket grinding against the asphalt, the weight on her spine, voices shouting above her. Then her memory breaks apart. She knows she was eventually released. She knows she walked to her car. The interval between those two facts is largely missing, a gap she cannot account for no matter how carefully she reaches back toward it. What she does have are pieces — a flash of a boot near her face, the particular scratch of riot-gear fabric against her wrist, the dark navy of a uniform filling her entire field of vision — but these pieces do not assemble into a coherent sequence. When she tries to tell the story, even to her daughter, she finds herself stopped not by emotion but by an absence of language, as though the experience exists in a register that words were not designed to reach.

In the months that followed, Priya's world contracted in ways that accumulated so gradually she did not at first recognize them as a pattern. She stopped attending the temple's community events, then stopped attending services altogether. She rerouted her daily errands to avoid the street where the demonstration had taken place. When a police cruiser appeared in her rearview mirror, her hands went cold on the steering wheel and her heart hammered in a way that felt wholly disproportionate and wholly uncontrollable. She had come to believe that her body was simply no longer trustworthy — that it would respond to the world with alarm regardless of what she consciously understood about her safety, and that this represented a permanent change in who she was.

Her professional life has been affected in ways that distress her deeply. Priya works closely with fabric samples, and on two separate occasions during client consultations she has encountered a coarsely woven textile — a heavy linen, a nubbled upholstery — and found herself unable to continue the meeting. She has not been able to explain this to clients in any way that preserves her professional standing, and she lost one significant contract when she abruptly ended a presentation. She has begun delegating the physical handling of fabric samples to her assistant, framing it as a matter of her arthritis, and she is aware of the deception this requires.

What frightens Priya most now is not any single symptom but a broader conclusion she has drawn about the remainder of her life. She is certain that nothing good can happen to her anymore — not in any meaningful sense — and that this is simply the truth of her situation rather than a distortion of it. When small difficulties arise, a delayed delivery, a miscommunication with a contractor, she finds herself flooded and unable to manage in ways that would once have been trivial, and this confirms her fear that whatever capacity she once had for resilience has been permanently spent.

It was her daughter who finally persuaded her to seek help, after Priya spent an evening unable to stop weeping following a television news segment that showed officers in uniform. Priya agreed to an intake appointment with considerable ambivalence. What she most hopes for, she said quietly at the end of her first session, is simply to be able to do her work again — to touch fabric without fear. What she most dreads is being told that she cannot.
